items.prompt: Before the fix, PATCH /api/tasks/[id] already ran updateMany with where { id, userId }. Why did Alice still manage to move her task into Bob's project?
items.answer: The where clause scoped the source task, and nothing checked the destination project
distractors: updateMany ignores the where clause when the data contains a foreign key column
Prisma's updateMany bypasses SQLite foreign-key constraints on related rows
The userId filter was applied after the write instead of before it ran
items.explanation: The where clause protects the source task row only; nothing checked who owned the destination project written via data: body. Authorization must cover every resource whose relationship the operation changes, not just the row being updated.

items.prompt: Alice's projects in area A have order 0, 2 and 5. She POSTs a new project to area A with no order field. What order does it get?
items.answer: 6, one more than the highest order among her projects in area A
distractors: 3, the count of projects that she already has in area A
0, because order is optional and new projects go first
1, the lowest order value in area A that is still unused
items.explanation: POST looks up her last project in that area by order desc and uses body.order ?? (last?.order ?? -1) + 1, so 5 + 1 = 6.

items.prompt: Why does the PATCH guard test body.projectId !== undefined instead of if (body.projectId)?
items.answer: An empty string is falsy yet still reaches updateMany, so it needs the lookup
distractors: The schema turns an omitted projectId into null, which a truthiness check misreads
TypeScript rejects truthiness checks on optional string fields at compile time
An undefined projectId means 'remove the task from its project' to this route
items.explanation: An empty string parses under z.string().optional() and would still reach updateMany via data: body, but a truthiness check would skip the lookup for it. Presence, not truthiness, decides whether the relationship changes. Authorization should never depend on favorable coercion.

items.prompt: Alice PATCHes her own task with only { title: 'New title' }. What does the route do?
items.answer: Skips the project lookup, runs the scoped updateMany, and returns the task (200)
distractors: Looks up the task's current project to confirm ownership, then runs the scoped update
Returns 400, because the patch schema requires projectId on each task write
Returns 404, because no project id was supplied for the destination guard to check
items.explanation: Omission means the request does not change the relationship, so no destination needs authorizing: updateMany runs scoped to { id, userId }, then the task is re-read and returned.

items.prompt: Where exactly does the POST /api/tasks ownership lookup run, and why does it select only id?
items.answer: Between taskSchema.parse and task.create, as it just needs existence
distractors: Before parsing, so that malformed bodies are rejected by the lookup itself
After task.create, so the new task's id can be included in the check
In one transaction with the create, which requires selecting every column
items.explanation: The guard sits between validation and the write and needs existence-within-scope, not the project object, so it selects only id; everything else in the create path (defaults, 201) is unchanged.

items.prompt: Why does the regression record every create/updateMany call and its arguments rather than only asserting a 404 status?
items.answer: A handler that wrote first and then returned 404 would still pass a status test
distractors: Status codes are unreliable inside Next.js route handler unit tests in Vitest
Recording calls is how the suite measures the guard's added performance overhead
The 404 body text changes between Prisma versions, so a status check is not enough
items.explanation: Such a handler would show the same status while still creating the forbidden relationship. The negative assertion that matters is that the forbidden relationship produces no task write.

items.prompt: You delete the POST guard at tasks/route.ts lines 38-44. The 'creates with the owned project' test still passes. What does that teach?
items.answer: A positive case alone misses a deleted guard, so a negative case is needed too
distractors: The owned-project test is redundant and should be deleted from the suite
The guard was dead code, since the create would have failed on its own
Status-code-only tests are sufficient for authorization whenever the case is positive
items.explanation: A positive case alone cannot detect a missing guard and a negative case alone cannot detect a guard that rejects everything - you need both. Only 'rejects a foreign project before create' fails, because it checks that no project read led to a create.

items.prompt: A POST /api/tasks body omits projectId entirely. What happens?
items.answer: taskSchema requires projectId, so parsing fails and the route returns 400
distractors: prisma.task.create runs without a project, and the ownership lookup is skipped
The lookup runs with an undefined id, so the route answers with a 404
The route assigns the user's default project and responds with a 201
items.explanation: Unlike PATCH, POST's taskSchema declares projectId: z.string() with no optional, so omission is a validation failure: a ZodError, a 400, and no lookup at all.

items.prompt: Alice PATCHes her own project with { areaId } set to the id of one of Bob's areas. What does PATCH /api/projects/[id] do?
items.answer: Returns 200, with her project now filed under Bob's area
distractors: Returns 404 'Project not found', as that area is not hers
Returns 400, since patchSchema does not accept an areaId
Returns 200, but areaId is dropped and her old area is kept
items.explanation: patchSchema allows areaId, and the updateMany is scoped only by the project's id and userId. Nothing checks who owns the area, so the write succeeds: one of the open findings in 06.

items.prompt: Alice has no tasks in Bob's project. She calls GET /api/tasks?projectId=<id of Bob's project>. What does she get back?
items.answer: 200 with an empty tasks list, as userId still filters the query
distractors: 404 'Project not found', from the same lookup that POST runs
200 with Bob's tasks in that project, as projectId is the filter
403, because that projectId belongs to another user's project
items.explanation: GET has no project lookup; it adds projectId to a where clause that always contains userId: auth.user.id and archived: false, so Bob's tasks never match.

items.prompt: Alice sends DELETE /api/tasks/[id] for one of her tasks. What happens to the task row?
items.answer: It stays with archived set to true, and GET /api/tasks stops listing it
distractors: It is removed, and the database cascades the delete to its day entries
It stays unchanged; only the client hides it until the next reload
It is removed only when no time entries still point at that task
items.explanation: DELETE runs task.updateMany({ where: { id, userId }, data: { archived: true } }) and returns { ok: true }. GET /api/tasks filters on archived: false.

items.prompt: Why doesn't the lookup-then-write gap let a project change owner between Alice's check and her write?
items.answer: Because no API path writes Project.userId, so the owner cannot change
distractors: Because the lookup and the write share a single prisma.$transaction
Because SQLite serializes writes, so the check and write cannot be interleaved
Because project ids are cuids that another user is unable to guess
items.explanation: The project PATCH schema allows only areaId, name and order, and settings import forces userId to the caller. Choose the mechanism from an actual invariant and failure scenario: only an ownership-transfer feature would require a composite FK or conditional insert.

items.front: Reviewer says 'PATCH already filters by userId, so the project check is redundant' (src/app/api/tasks/[id]/route.ts:23-36). Give the counterexample.
items.back: Alice owns task A; Bob owns project B. Alice PATCHes A with projectId B. updateMany({ where: { id: A, userId: Alice } }) matches, so without the guard A points into Bob's project. The project query needs { id: B, userId: Alice }, the task write needs { id: A, userId: Alice }: neither predicate replaces the other.

items.front: The worked change fixed tasks only. Name the bug class still open in POST /api/daytask (src/app/api/daytask/route.ts:33-42) and its siblings.
items.back: Unchecked relationship ids: body.taskId (and goalId, areaId elsewhere) is written without looking the target up with the caller's userId. Once a DayTask points at Bob's task, GET /api/day's includes turn the write into a read leak of Bob's task, project and area names.

items.front: Write the shape of the destination ownership guard used in POST /api/tasks (src/app/api/tasks/route.ts:38-44).
items.back: findFirst({ where: { id: body.projectId, userId: auth.user.id }, select: { id: true } }); if nothing comes back, return 404 'Project not found' before any write. One predicate pair proves the relationship is allowed at that moment.

items.front: What does handleError (src/lib/api.ts:13-29) return for a ZodError, for any other Error, and for a non-Error throw?
items.back: ZodError: 400 'Validation failed' with the issues. Any other Error: 400 with error.message verbatim - which is how raw Prisma constraint messages leak to clients. Anything else: 500 'Unknown error'.
